questions.q: What is the central conflict that the "image" device externalizes in "Broken Images"?
questions.a: The "image" device externalizes Manjula's internal conflict between her public persona (the confident, successful English novelist addressing a TV audience) and her private truth (guilt over her sister Malini, resentment over parental favoritism, insecurity about writing in English, and marital distance). A wrong answer that only identifies the language debate (Kannada vs English) misses the deeper psychological split — the image isn't just about language politics; it's about the fracture between who Manjula performs as and who she actually is.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the play's title "Broken Images" (referencing T.S. Eliot's "The Waste Land") is an appropriate metaphor for Manjula's situation.
questions.a: The title "Broken Images" reflects how Manjula's identity exists as fragmented, disconnected pieces — the Kannada writer, the English novelist, the devoted sister, the resentful sibling, the loyal wife, the abandoned partner — that never cohere into a whole. Like Eliot's "heap of broken images" where "the dead tree gives no shelter," Manjula's constructed selves offer no genuine refuge; each image is a performance that collapses under scrutiny. A wrong answer that only explains the Eliot reference without connecting it to Manjula's specific fractures (language, sister, marriage, success) shows superficial understanding.

questions.q: Apply the concept of "primary theme" to identify ONE sentence from Manjula's TV speech that encapsulates the play's central concern, and explain how the Image's later dialogue undermines it.
questions.a: Manjula says: "I am a Kannada writer myself, born to the language and civilization, and proud of it." This encapsulates the primary theme of performed identity. The Image later undermines it by revealing Manjula's admission: "I could not have written about my sister in Kannada. She breathed, laughed, dreamt in English" — exposing that Manjula's "Kannada writer" identity is a chosen performance, not an organic truth. A wrong answer that picks a sentence about Malini or Pramod without showing how the Image contradicts it fails to demonstrate the theme of image vs. reality.

questions.q: Analyze how the shift from monologue to dialogue structures the revelation of the primary theme. Why must the play begin as a monologue?
questions.a: The play begins as a monologue to establish Manjula's controlled public performance — the "image" she projects to the world. The shift to dialogue (when the Image speaks back) shatters that control, forcing the private truth into the open. The monologue format mirrors the TV interview: one-way, curated, safe. The dialogue format mirrors psychological confrontation: two-way, uncontrolled, exposing. If the play began as dialogue, the theme of "image vs. reality" would have no structure to break; the monologue-first structure makes the fracture visible. A wrong answer that only describes the structural change without explaining its thematic function misses the analytical point.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "Manjula's writing in English is a betrayal of Kannada." Use evidence from both the TV speech and the Image dialogue to defend or critique this claim.
questions.a: The claim is the play's central debate, but the play critiques the claim itself. In her speech, Manjula defends writing in English as organic ("it burst out in English") and notes the hypocrisy of critics who speak English while condemning it. The Image dialogue deepens this: Manjula admits she "tried to occupy [Kannada] and make it mine" because Malini "breathed, laughed, dreamt in English" — suggesting English was the language of their shared intimate world, not a colonial imposition. The play evaluates the "betrayal" charge as a reductive political slogan that ignores the complex, lived bilingual reality of Indian writers. A wrong answer that simply agrees or disagrees without showing how the play complicates the binary fails the evaluation task.

questions.q: Create a 4-line dialogue between Manjula and her Image that could occur AFTER the play ends, revealing a new fracture in her identity not explicitly discussed in the text.
questions.a:
MANJULA: The royalties paid for Malini's care. That was the deal.
IMAGE: And the film rights? The Koramangala house sale? Who did those pay for?
MANJULA: Pramod's LA apartment. My silence.
IMAGE: A heap of broken images. And the dead tree gives no shelter.
A good answer creates a dialogue that (a) uses the Image's voice as internal truth-teller, (b) introduces a new material transaction (film rights, house sale), (c) connects to the Eliot epigraph, and (d) reveals a new fracture (financial complicity, marital transaction). A poor answer writes generic emotional lines without textual grounding or thematic extension.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The primary theme of a literary work is its central, unifying idea or message that the author conveys through the narrative, ______, and dramatic structure.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you're scrolling through social media and see a celebrity's perfect post — then you read a leaked private message ______ their real struggles.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can identify the primary theme of "Broken Images," trace its development through the monologue-dialogue structure, and explain how the image device externalizes Manjula's internal conflict between her Kannada identity and English success, supporting their analysis with specific textual evidence.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine you're ______ through social media and see a celebrity's perfect post — then you read a leaked private message revealing their real struggles.
